adult.how: Scenes come from work and daily life (a colleague handling something for you, moving house, borrowing things); add the honorific layer (くださる, いただく) and the viewpoint of passive-causatives, show terms directly and compare with the first language. Step 3 is three or four sentences with a consistent viewpoint, such as telling a manager who helped with what.
adult.watch: The adult takes care with honorifics but shifts viewpoint mid-account, moving "I" twice in one sentence.

child.how: Checking which kinds of clause can follow and naming the constraint that was broken is explicit analysis of grammatical form, which is generally not the right main activity under 12, and not at all for ages 5–7. At this age children should first use connectives as whole chunks in sequencing and retelling (first... then..., when...) and hear and say them often before constraints come up. Children of 8–12 can sometimes play "story chain": the first half of a sentence with a picture, two cards for the second half ("please..." / "then this happened..."), one connective only, no constraint names.
child.watch: Asked to explain why a clause cannot follow, the child memorises a rule instead of learning to use the connective.

youth.how: Fix the first clause and let students try each second-clause card, sum up the constraint from the results, and only then get the terms. Situations come from their lives (inviting friends, travel plans, exam-week planning). State the reverse half directly: constraints have exceptions, and each set includes at least one item that breaks the surface pattern. Step 3 is a sentence ending in a request or intention. Show secondary students what these items look like on exams.
youth.watch: Students know the constraint table by heart but cannot produce one natural sentence that ends with a request.

adult.how: Situations come from work email and travel arrangements; the constraint table is shown with its terms (expressions of intention, requests, established facts), the rule comes first and then the test. Step 3 writes two sentences for the same situation using two different connectives that both work. Adults most often go wrong in the request sentence of an email, so take items from there.
adult.watch: The adult maps the first-language "if... then..." onto one connective and uses it for every conditional.

child.how: For ages 5–8 and heritage children who speak but do not yet read: pictures come from the child's home, pets and toys; the child says a sentence, an adult writes it under the picture, and the child follows the words with a finger while hearing it played back. At most three new characters or words at a time; the word wall is a tree that grows a leaf each time one is recognised. The reverse half gets one item each for same-sounding and look-alike words (在/再, was/saw). Reading to a parent is the main output; no writing required.
child.watch: The child "reads" their own card by remembering what they said, and cannot recognise the word in a new combination.

youth.how: For teenagers raised abroad who speak the heritage language well but read and write it poorly: topics come from family talk, friends' messages, shows they watch. Step 2 adds same-sounding characters (在/再, 的/得) and the written form of spoken words (啥 → 什么). The word wall becomes a personal word list they can match against their own chats. No childish pictures, and do not put them on a beginner's pace.
youth.watch: Fluent in speech, the teenager assumes they "more or less" read and write too, skips the same-sound items in step 2, and writes full of homophone errors.

adult.how: For adult heritage speakers who speak but cannot read or write: topics come from family, work, menus and text messages, and step 2 adds same-sounding characters and replacing spoken words with written ones. Each short unit ends with being able to read one real thing (a menu, a stretch of the family group chat). Absolute-beginner adults do not have these words in speech, so it does not apply; start them with phonics or character anatomy.
adult.watch: The adult feels that learning to read is "like primary school" and avoids reading aloud, reading silently so that misreadings go unnoticed.

child.how: The core pre-reading activity for ages 5–7: clapping and hopping, words from animals and food, sound and pictures only. Each set does one operation (only rhymes, or only clapping syllables); a new game means a new activity. The reverse half is a pair that looks like it should rhyme but does not, and a pair that differs only in tone. In step 3 a teacher or parent is the listener; 8–12 year olds who can already blend do not need it.
child.watch: The child claps along with the adult and gets it right by following their rhythm, not by counting the beats.

youth.how: For teenagers, drop rhyming games and practise only the layer they really struggle with: mora timing in Japanese (とうきょう, コーヒー, きって), or segmenting English words to stop adding vowels after consonants. Material is place names, loanwords and brand names; terms like mora, syllable and phoneme can be used, and it can be set up as a rhythm challenge. The listener is a classmate.
youth.watch: Students count syllables and clap とうきょう as two beats, because nobody made clear that a mora is not a syllable.

adult.how: Adults use it the same way: mora timing for learners of Japanese, phoneme segmentation for people correcting added vowels in English; words from place names and loanwords, with terms shown directly. A few minutes at a time, as a warm-up or repair before another activity rather than a main thread. No children's pictures or animation.
adult.watch: The adult finds it too easy and skips it, then keeps dropping a beat on long vowels and double consonants.

child.how: Only for literate 8–12 year olds: one character with two readings at a time (长 cháng/zhǎng, 大人 おとな), with two pictures for the two meanings and just one question, "is it about length or growing up?"; no terms for the basis. Ages 5–7 skip it. Step 3 becomes saying one sentence for each reading from pictures. Keep one reverse-half item that just has to be memorised.
child.watch: The child pairs each reading with its picture and stops looking at the sentence.

youth.how: Secondary school is when learners meet most multi-reading characters, on/kun readings and English stress shift: let them find the basis from example sentences first, then name it. Material is textbook passages, lyrics, titles and names. In step 3 they write a sentence using one form with two readings and can set it for a classmate. High-frequency exam items are marked separately.
youth.watch: Students treat tendencies like "nouns stressed first, verbs second" as iron rules and apply them to hotel.

adult.how: Material is headlines, station names, menus and personal names; the basis is shown with its terms (on and kun readings, special kanji readings, rendaku, alternate readings, stress shift). Adults draw on their first language, and Chinese speakers who read Japanese kanji by their Chinese sound need this compared directly. Step 3 asks them to explain the basis for each of the two readings.
adult.watch: Chinese-speaking adults guess Japanese readings from the Chinese sound, and the few lucky guesses make them check less and less.

child.how: Only for literate 8–12 year olds whose two languages share characters or loanwords (for example a Chinese-reading child learning Japanese): three words per set, the two meanings shown as pictures (手紙 as a letter and as a toilet roll), and the three levels shown as "same / a bit different / totally different" faces. The child says the guessed meaning first, then checks with the picture. The reverse half matters most: include plenty of "same" words so the child learns that most of them can be borrowed. Ages 5–7 skip it.
child.watch: Having learned one or two funny false friends, the child decides every shared word is a trap.

youth.how: A standard activity for Chinese secondary and university students learning Japanese, or English-background students learning French or Spanish: write the guess first, then judge from real example sentences. Examples come from the manga, news and lyrics they read; the four kinds of shift are found from examples before being named. A shared class list of false friends can include the "same meaning" words too.
youth.watch: Students distrust every Sino-Japanese word, reading slows down, and they look up even 学生 and 問題.

adult.how: Example sentences come from news, business email and rental contracts; the kinds of shift are named directly, and katakana loanwords and the more formal register of Sino-Japanese words are included. Adults bring a lot of first-language knowledge, so use the positive transfer: say up front that most words match, then focus on the shifted and totally different ones. Step 3 is two sentences in a work or daily-life situation.
adult.watch: The adult gets the meaning right but misses the register shift and uses a very formal Sino-Japanese word with friends.

child.how: The source is a picture with two or three simple sentences, and the child only does mediation like "help a friend tell their mum"; no terms for adding or removing, just "what does mum have to know from this?", with stickers on the key information. Suits ages 8–12; children in heritage-language families often really do relay things for relatives. Ages 5–7 relay one sentence orally. Reverse half: one name or number cannot be reworded.
child.watch: When relaying, the child adds things the source did not say, or drops key pieces such as the time and place.

youth.how: Use material they would really relay: school notices for parents, update notes for a game or app, messages from friends abroad, news clips. They split and align first, find adding, cutting and rewording in examples, then name them. Step 3 relays to a given person (a parent who does not speak the language, friends in a group chat). Show where a translation app's word-for-word draft sounds unnatural.
youth.watch: Students paste in the translation app's output, and the "change at least one chunk" in step 1 is just a synonym swap.

adult.how: Sources are work emails, contract clauses, meeting remarks or news clips; treatments are named with their terms (addition, omission, shift). Adults often relay things for colleagues or family, so step 3 can specify a written or an oral channel, the oral one being a timed relay then transcribed. Practice translations must not be used externally for official legal or medical texts.
adult.watch: The adult treats politeness and softening as "carrying no information" and cuts them, so the relay reads as blunt.

child.how: Only for 8–12 year olds who know numbers up to a thousand: numbers stay under ten thousand, blocks or coins show "ten thousand is ten thousands", and million never appears. Estimating size becomes "about how many piles is this?". Step 3 is saying one number from home or school (how many pupils, the price of a toy). Ages 5–7 practise counting itself, without conversion.
child.watch: The child can read out the digits one by one but has no sense of how big the number is, so the estimate is a random tap.

youth.how: Use numbers they care about: view counts, follower counts, ticket prices, city populations, tuition. Let them compare the two ways of grouping digits and find the conversion rule before it is stated; add percentages and approximate words. Step 3 is saying a large number from their own life using the other language's place values.
youth.watch: The student converts correctly with a calculator but swaps ten thousand and a hundred thousand when saying it aloud.

adult.how: Adults meet large numbers every day at work and in life: news, financial reports, house prices, budgets, statistics, including 億 and billion, percentages, tenths (成), decimals and currencies. State the rule directly and compare it with first-language grouping. Step 3 is a full sentence with an approximate number, used in a real email or report.
adult.watch: In a meeting the adult converts "fifteen ten-thousands" into their first language before understanding it and falls behind the conversation.

child.how: Only "spot it" and "where would you hear it": cartoon characters stand for regions (a British child says biscuit, an American child says cookie), and the child drags each phrase to its speaker. Children are not asked to produce varieties other than the one they are learning, and nobody judges which is better. Reverse half: one phrase is the same everywhere. Ages 5–7 work entirely by sound and pictures.
child.watch: One region's character is drawn as funnier or more "correct", and the child learns that some accents are lower rather than that varieties differ.

youth.how: Teenagers meet many varieties through series, games and the internet: use those sources, let them sort expressions into columns themselves, then discuss settings. Step 3 writes for a given setting and keeps to one variety throughout (a comment for Taiwanese users online, an application essay in British spelling). Reverse half: one item that looks like a variety but is an error. Accents are never ranked.
youth.watch: Students mix British and American spelling, or simplified and traditional characters, in one essay and do not care because both are "correct".

adult.how: Adults have real audiences: product information for the Taiwanese market, British official documents, clients in Kansai, colleagues in Hong Kong. Discuss why one text should stay consistent; step 3 includes converting a whole passage between simplified and traditional characters and making spelling consistent. Point out the errors conversion tools make (one simplified character mapping to several traditional ones).
adult.watch: The adult converts simplified to traditional in one click without checking one-to-many characters and regional vocabulary.

child.how: Only for ages 8–12, only metaphors and idioms, no irony: first look at a picture of the literal meaning (literally adding legs to a drawn snake), have a laugh, then choose another picture for what it really means. Ages 5–7 just hear a line from a story and see the literal and real pictures. Reverse half: one line looks figurative but is literal (it really is pouring).
child.watch: Having learned that "this doesn't mean what it says", the child reads every unfamiliar phrase as figurative.

youth.how: Use material they know: internet slang, memes, lyrics, anime lines, dialogue in novels, including irony and implication. Write the literal layer first, judge the gap, then point to the clues. Discuss whether an expression belongs in an essay; for secondary students separate exam questions on rhetoric from real communication.
youth.watch: Students carry the implied meanings of memes into formal writing, or over-read places that need a literal reading.

adult.how: Contexts come from novels, commentary and business conversations (polite refusals like 「検討します」, 「前向きに考えます」), including narrator irony. What adults most need is to hear a polite refusal at work, so step 3 asks whether the expression belongs in formal writing and meetings. Compare with first-language equivalents.
adult.watch: The adult takes 「前向きに考えます」 ("we'll consider it positively") as a yes and moves ahead on the literal meaning.

child.how: Picking a sense from a multi-sense dictionary entry and giving reasons for rejecting the others belongs to the reading-to-learn stage; it is usually not a main activity under 12, and 5–7 year olds should not do it. First use context guessing in an illustrated story: one word appears several times and the child points to pictures and revises. Children of 8–12 can sometimes use a picture dictionary (bat as a bat for games and as an animal), tapping the picture that fits the sentence, with only the most common plural and -ing endings to undo.
child.watch: The child always lands on the first sense and takes it as the only meaning.

youth.how: Students start reading lots of authentic material and using dictionaries and translation apps: use learner-dictionary entries, with sentences from what they are reading. Point out that a translation app usually gives one sense, and here they learn to choose against the context. Sort the five reasons for rejecting a sense from examples first. In step 3 they rephrase the sense in their own words, put it back in the sentence and note it in their word book.
youth.watch: The student pastes the whole sentence into a translation app and works backwards from the translation instead of choosing in the entry.

adult.how: Use full learner-dictionary entries (register labels, collocation boxes, usage notes), including phrasal verbs and multi-sense function words; sentences come from work documents and news the learner must read. State the reverse half directly (sometimes you have to go to the phrase entry). In step 3 the record is exported to their personal phrase book.
adult.watch: The adult lingers on every multi-sense word, looking up sentence after sentence until reading becomes dictionary work.

child.how: Input-method conversion needs pinyin or romaji spelling, recognition of the target characters and regular keyboard use, which most children under 12 do not yet have; 5–7 year olds should not do it at all. First get characters recognised and written: practise with character anatomy, and handle same-sounding characters (在/再, 他/她/它) in reading with pictures. Children of 8–12 who already type pinyin can do a three-option character pick only, with no whole-sentence typing on their own.
child.watch: The child always taps the first candidate, which looks fast but involves no choosing at all.

youth.how: Teenagers type and chat every day, so this is how they really write: sentences come from chats, comments, homework and their own posts. Same-sound errors in step 2 can be taken from their own chats (anonymised) or swapped with a classmate to find each other's. For Chinese students learning Japanese, focus on simplified characters slipping into Japanese and the boundary of okurigana. Step 3 is one sentence typed independently with frequency ordering switched off.
youth.watch: Used to predictive completion, the student lets the whole sentence appear from suggestions without making a single choice.

adult.how: Use real sentences: email, work chat, forms, addresses, with proper nouns and multi-segment conversion; for Japanese add okurigana boundaries (変える/替える) and Chinese–Japanese character forms getting mixed up. Step 3 can be timed to match how fast real replies are written. The learner leaves with a list of their own frequent same-sound mistakes.
adult.watch: Typing Japanese at work with a Chinese input method, the adult gets Chinese character forms mixed in and cannot see it.

child.how: Only two or three kinds of trouble (too fast, an unknown word, didn't catch it), and two or three fixed repair phrases with gesture pictures (ear = say it again, snail = slower please). No time window; in step 3 the teacher plays the other person and says one line too fast on purpose. Reverse half: one word the teacher is about to explain, so there is no need to interrupt. These repair phrases are chunks a child should have from the very start.
child.watch: When the child does not understand they just nod and say "yes", because adults usually carry on anyway.

youth.how: Pretending to understand is the most common problem at this age. Use their situations: chatting with an exchange student, online voice chat, part-time work, group work in class. They review what they did at each trouble moment before the repair types are named. Step 3 is practice with a partner using role cards, the partner speaking fast or using a new word at the marked points. Explain that the other person's "mm" or はい usually just means "I'm listening".
youth.watch: Not wanting to look lost in front of classmates, the student picks "backchannel and carry on" at every trouble moment.

adult.how: Phone calls, meetings, clinic visits, adding interrupting, steering back, buying time and summarising others; the time window is close to a real pause. Adults can practise privately against the script until confident, then move to a real partner; step 3 requires at least one confirmation by paraphrase. These moves are what keeps an adult afloat in real conversations and are worth learning early.
adult.watch: The adult feels it is rude to ask someone to repeat, guesses or checks a recording later, and gets the key information wrong.

child.how: A library card, a birthday invitation, a note to family; only three or four fields, icons showing what goes in each, letter cards allowed for writing; the only judgements are "done right / something missing". Ages 5–7 write only their name and draw; an adult writes the rest. Reverse half: one field can be left empty. Situation cards use made-up identities.
child.watch: The child copies the sample card word for word, and on a new invitation the date and place are still the sample's.

youth.how: Formats they meet: club sign-up forms, exchange programme applications, emails to teachers, shift notes at a part-time job, chat messages. They write first, then check field by field, guessing first "what does the person reading this field use it for?". Step 3 writes the same thing to a friend and to a teacher. No real personal information.
youth.watch: Students email a teacher in chat style, or message a friend with a letter opening.

adult.how: Sign-up forms, rental registration, leave-request emails, messages to a teacher or client, rescheduling texts: all things adults really write. The same matter goes to two kinds of recipient, with a note on how the versions differ. Use made-up identities and no real ID details. Short units, one form or one message.
adult.watch: The adult fills in fields by first-language conventions (name order, date format, address order), so the content is right but the reader is confused.
